narrative:
The model estimated a 25% chance that you would be a bad credit risk. In practical terms, that is roughly one chance in four of repayment difficulty; the bank’s decision rule treated that risk as too high, so your application was denied.

The three most influential factors in your assessment were your savings status, your property status, and your installment rate. Your savings information—recorded as unknown/none, a category shared by about one-third of approved applicants—was the strongest factor, and it pushed the assessment toward good credit. Your real estate property was the second strongest and also pushed toward good credit; real estate is held by about one-third of approved applicants. Your installment rate of 1% of disposable income, well below the approved average of about 3%, was third and also helped your case. These favorable top factors are why the estimated bad-credit probability stayed relatively low.

The denial therefore reflects the combined effect of the remaining profile details, not these three leading factors; other aspects, such as the requested amount being much higher than the approved average and your current employment being unemployed, added risk.

Next, ask the bank for a human review or appeal and for the specific policy reasons for denial. Consider reducing the requested amount, adding a guarantor or co-applicant, correcting any savings-record errors, and reapplying after establishing stable employment. A credit counselor can help you prioritize these steps.
